name: Rosa
lede: Rosa is the Latin word for the rose and the plain word for pink in Spanish, Portuguese and German; as a color name here it is a bright screen pink with no documented maker.

sections.title: A word for pink, not for roses
sections.body:
*Rosa* is the Latin word for the rose, and in Spanish, Portuguese and German it is also the everyday word for the color pink [1]. In Spanish the color is *rosa*, in Portuguese *cor-de-rosa*, in German *rosa* [1]. Italian uses it too: the leader's jersey in the Giro d'Italia is the *maglia rosa*, a pink one [2]. In English the color is [[pink]], and that word has a different story [1].

Where this particular swatch got its name is undocumented. Our library finds it in two sources, a wiki list and the xkcd color survey of 2010, and neither says why it was called Rosa [8]. By distance, its nearest named neighbors are [[schauss-pink]], [[salmon-pink]], [[pale-dogwood]] and [[pink]], at 2.6, 3.2, 4.0 and 4.4 CIEDE2000 units [8]. The ISCC-NBS category closest to it is "vivid pink" [8].

sections.title: The rose that was not pink
sections.body:
The Latin adjective *roseus* sounds like "rosy", but Pastoureau calls it a false friend: it meant bright red, vermilion, a very beautiful red [1]. Romans used it for women's makeup and for cloth dyed with kermes [1]. The Greeks and Romans saw pink in flowers, rocks and dawn skies, and Pastoureau argues they never gave the color a name of its own [1].

Homer's "rosy-fingered" dawn is the reddish light of sunrise, not a flower and not our pink [1]. Even the roses of antiquity were almost never pink; they were red, white or sometimes yellow [1]. In medieval Latin, *roseus* still meant vermilion, and in Old French the adjective *rose* was rare and could mean pale, beige or yellowish [1].

sections.title: How pink got its names
sections.body:
Pink arrived through a dye. Brazilwood, a wood imported from Asia, had long been considered impermanent as a dye [1]. Around 1380 to 1400, Italian dyers found mordants that made it more stable and gave truly pink shades [1]. Painters turned the dyestuff into lake pigments, and the color needed a name [1]. Venetian and Tuscan *incarnato*, meaning flesh-colored, became the term, and it gave French *incarnat*, Spanish *encarnado* and English *carnation* [1]. Our name list still keeps [[carnation]] [8].

From the fifteenth to the seventeenth century, European charts treated this new color as a pale yellow, since the slot between white and red was already taken by yellow [1]. The French adjective *rose* is absent from dictionaries before the middle of the eighteenth century, and the Académie française did not list it until its sixth edition in 1835 [1]. Pastoureau dates the modern pink to the mid-1700s, when Madame de Pompadour made it the fashion, and when roses that were truly rose, unknown in antiquity, had become common through breeding [1]. In Spanish, Portuguese and German the color word also took until the nineteenth century to settle, and English *pink* long meant only the brazilwood dye [1].

A last correction: pink was not always a girls' color. In the eighteenth century it was often worn by men and boys, and the firm split of pink for girls and blue for boys dates from the 1930s [1].

sections.title: Rosa in the paintbox
sections.body:
Painters knew *rosa* long before the color name settled. A sixteenth-century Italian recipe term, *roza* or *rosa*, stood for [[madder]], with *roza di Fiandra* as a variant [3]. *Terra rosa*, "rose earth", was Church's name for red ochre, whose pinkish red comes from ferric oxide, and Mayer ties it to Venetian red [3]. Neither is the pale pink of today, and both point to red rather than to the flower [3].

Another Rosa is a person, and the name has nothing to do with the color [4]. Gage lists Salvator Rosa with Claude and Poussin among the earlier landscape painters whom Romantic artists looked back to [4]. The Pigment Compendium names him among the Roman artists of the seventeenth century linked to lead-tin-antimony yellows [10]. See [[painter:salvator-rosa|Salvator Rosa]] for the painter.

sections.title: Roses in the naturalists' charts
sections.body:
Werner's nomenclature, as edited by Patrick Syme in 1821, has a "Rose Red", number 89 [5]. Syme defines it as carmine red with a great quantity of white and a very small portion of cochineal red, and points to the common garden rose and to flamingo feathers [5]. The French rose, *Rosa gallica*, stands for his darker "Lake Red" and "Purplish Red" [5]. In 1797 the Swiss chemist Henri Struve described a red, *Rouge de kinorodon*, as the fruit of the sweet briar, though Baty remarks that the fruit of the dog rose would match it better [6].

The word also lives in a festival. The Spanish town of Consuegra holds a Rosa del Azafrán festival every October, and Finlay reports that a tourist delegation from Toledo invented it in 1962 [7]. It celebrates the harvest behind [[saffron-yellow]] [7].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here, #FE86A4, is a bright, slightly cool pink on screens [8]. It is a modern screen color, not a historical dye: the first record we hold is the 2010 survey [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This pink is absent from the museum. No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within four CIEDE2000 units of it covering even one per cent of the canvas [9]. The same is true of [[pink]], [[carnation]] and [[schauss-pink]] [9]. That describes our archive of photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not painting as a whole [9].

So the bright pink of the screen is a color that museum paintings, as photographed, do not hold at that strength [9]. The books add that brazilwood dye was long considered impermanent, so fading may play a part, though no archive count can separate it from the painters' own choices [1][9].

origin.named_after: origin of this swatch name undocumented; the word is Latin rosa, rose

disambiguation.gloss: Syme's and Ridgway's rose red is a deeper crimson-pink, not this bright screen pink

questions.q: What did the Latin adjective roseus mean?
True or false: the English word pink first named a dyestuff from brazilwood, before it named a color.
Why was pink treated as a shade of yellow in European charts for two centuries?
choices: The place between white and red was already held by yellow
Pink had no connection to red in Latin
Brazilwood dye turned yellow with age
questions.answer: The place between white and red was already held by yellow

openers: The Latin word for rose did not mean pink: roseus meant bright red.
Pink was a boy's color in the eighteenth century; the girl-blue split dates from the 1930s.
This bright pink does not appear at one per cent of the canvas in any of our 23,781 paintings.
